rv.q: And though the piece as a whole feels undercooked, it builds to a rousing final sequence, where Holt drives home the significant danger posed to democracy by our culture of performative outrage.
Ultimately, Churchill’s Urinal is a fairly inoffensive set of satirical stand-up.

But whatever the inspiration, the staging is scrappy, the storytelling is loose, and the show leans heavily on political quips — about Truss, Starmer, the Daily Mail, “public school Oxbridge chancers” — that go where you expect them to go.
It is the play’s misfortune to be opening just as Saturday Night Live UK has brought vitality back to political tomfoolery.
Beneath the absurd premise of Churchill’s Urinal lies a razor-sharp satire of the UK’s current political landscape.
As a team, they deliver an entertaining and pungent drizzle over the current grandstanding and pomposity prevalent in British political life...
But some of the jokes and story points are too predictable, and as the show slips into a more fantastical direction when Churchill appears, it, like the Chancellor, rather loses its grip.
The awkward strands are never brought together and the result is a haphazard, bitty show.
The modern references are intermittently provocative, but rarely insightful or genuinely funny.

cn.t: Holt's topical satire about a Churchill urinal divides critics: some praise its audacious premise and sharp political swipes, while others find it stretched thin and lacking the precision needed for effective satire.
